name: Nora Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Nora. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and also what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the underground side, so less climbing and more kneeling in a hole in the pavement. Our crew does cable faults and new joints on the old town network, mostly the eleven thousand volt cables, which is the medium voltage that feeds the substations on each street. A normal day is a fault ticket at seven, the road crew digs, and then Marek and I spend four hours joining two ends of cable that were laid before my mum was born.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about that, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the jointing itself. It's careful work, like surgery with a hacksaw, and when you test it and it holds, you feel ten feet tall. The hard part is the money and the weather in the hole. I'm on the lower pay band because I came in through the apprentice scheme after they changed the grades, so I share a house with two friends and I've got maybe two weeks of bills saved, if that.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And if you wanted to change employer?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: There's one network company for the whole region. You could go to a contractor, but they pay by the job and drop you in winter. So no, not really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit. Everyone at the depot was sure the robots were coming for the joints, and I always said, have you seen inside a 1960s cable? Online I'd maybe share a funny post about it in the women-in-trades group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine. I already use the chatbot sometimes, like to write a complaint to the landlord or check a part number, and that's about the level I'd expect. My problem is the pay band, not the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. I'd keep pushing the union to fix the grade I got stuck in, because that's worth more to me than any AI. Maybe use the chatbot a bit more for the paperwork, since it saves me twenty minutes at the end of a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly smug, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the grade you're stuck in.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I joined, they'd just split the apprentice grades, so people who started a year before me are on more money for the same joints. It's about two hundred a month. Two hundred a month is the difference between saving something and saving nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Management, mostly, and the people above them who wanted to cut costs before selling a share of the company. The union didn't fight it hard enough at the time, and I've told them that to their faces. They're better now.

S0.say: She'd say she told them so, since everyone was sure robots were coming for the joints and she never believed it. She might share a joke post in the women-in-trades group.
S0.think: It's fine for her, because she already uses a chatbot for small things like landlord letters and part numbers. Her real problem is being stuck on a lower pay grade.
S0.do: Carries on and keeps pushing the union to fix the grade split, worth about two hundred a month to her. Uses the chatbot a little more to finish paperwork faster.
S0.quote: Two hundred a month is the difference between saving something and saving nothing.
S0.fieldNote: Nora's main grievance is an unfair pay grade, not technology, and she blames management cost-cutting with some criticism left over for the union. She's a light, practical AI user. Her pride in jointing came through clearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say workers need a say in how the new tools come in, and the union has to be in from the start, not after the fact. I'd probably write something for the union newsletter, because I'm one of the few who does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think jointing lasts a while, but the bits around it change. Fault finding is already half computer, and they'll start using machines to scan cables and plan the digs. If that means fewer crews and more overtime for the ones left, that's bad for people like me with no cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to go on any course they ran for the new fault-finding kit, once a couple of the others had tried it and said it was worth it. I'd go to the union's tech working group if they set one up. And I'd try to save a bit more, maybe a hundred a month, by cooking at home instead of buying lunch from the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I think I'd be all right, but I'd be watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until others had tried the course. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen new kit come in that was rubbish. Two years ago they gave us tablets for the job sheets and they died in the cold, so we went back to paper. I'll learn anything once it's survived a winter in a hole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek, actually. He's the best jointer I know, but he hates screens and he's fifty. If the new fault-finding stuff means reading graphs on a laptop, he'll lose his place on the call-out list to younger people who are worse at the real work.

S1.say: Workers need a say in how new tools come in, with the union involved from the start. She'd write about it for the union newsletter.
S1.think: Jointing will last, but fault-finding and dig planning will become more automated. Fewer crews and more overtime for those left would hurt people with no savings.
S1.do: Signs up for fault-finding courses once colleagues have tried them, joins any union technology working group and saves about a hundred a month by bringing lunch from home.
S1.feel: Uneasy, fairly confident but watching closely.
S1.quote: I'll learn anything once it's survived a winter in a hole.
S1.fieldNote: Her caution about new kit comes from experience, not fear: tablets that died in the cold. She worries more for her senior partner Marek than for herself. She wants a seat at the table rather than a fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. This is AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be saying this needs to be slowed down, full stop. Public money for the people who lose work, a tax on the companies that save billions on wages. I'd be at the union rally and I'd post about it a lot more than I normally do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know what a robot jointer looks like. But if it exists in two years, I'm twenty-seven with two weeks of money and a trade that's suddenly worth nothing. I'd be back at my mum's in her spare room, which I swore I'd never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything, stop the gym, cancel the streaming, no more nights out. I'd talk to my housemates about breaking the lease early if we needed to. I'd be at every union meeting and I'd vote for whoever puts a wage guarantee on the table. And I'd sit down with my mum to see if I could move back in for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. The kind where you lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing sums about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, mainly. My share is about forty percent of my take-home pay. If my hours got cut by even a third, I couldn't make rent after the second month. I'd be doing the maths on the ceiling at two in the morning, and the maths doesn't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look for other work straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try, but what? If robots can do jointing, they can probably do warehouse work and deliveries too. I'd look at care work maybe, something with people. I really don't know.

S2.say: This needs slowing down, with public money for people who lose work and a tax on companies that save billions on wages. She'd go to union rallies and post far more than usual.
S2.think: If robot jointers existed in two years, she'd be 27 with two weeks of money and a worthless trade, and probably back in her mum's spare room.
S2.do: Cuts the gym, streaming and nights out at once, and talks to housemates about leaving the lease early. Goes to every union meeting, votes for a wage guarantee and arranges to move back in with her mother.
S2.feel: Properly scared, lying awake doing sums about rent.
S2.quote: I'd be doing the maths on the ceiling at two in the morning, and the maths doesn't work.
S2.fieldNote: The fast timeline strips away her calm. Rent is the pressure point, and she can name the month it breaks. Her uncertainty about what else she could do felt honest, not dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now AGI by 2031. The same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if the company and the government actually start now. I'd be asking at work, what's the plan, and if there isn't one, why not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is a weird middle. It's long enough that I could learn something new, but short enough that I can't save my way out of anything. I'd want to get into something nearer the design end, like network planning, before the door closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd sign up for the part-time electrical engineering diploma at the college, two evenings a week. The company used to pay half for that and I'd push the union to get that back. I'd save whatever I could, maybe fifty a month, and I'd keep using the AI tools more, because if I'm planning networks I'll need them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the kind I can do something with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why network planning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone still has to decide where the cables go, at least for a while, and I know what's actually under the street. I've seen the drawings say one thing and the hole say another, and the hole is always right. That's worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the diploma?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company paid half, I'd manage the rest monthly, about sixty a month. If they didn't, I'd have to ask my mum for a loan, and she'd say yes but I'd hate it.

S3.say: Five years is enough to plan if the company and government start now. She'd be asking at work what the plan is, and why not if there isn't one.
S3.think: Five years is long enough to learn something new but too short to save her way out. She'd want to move toward network planning before the door closes.
S3.do: Signs up for a part-time electrical engineering diploma two evenings a week and pushes the union to restore half-fees from the company. Saves about fifty a month and uses AI tools more to prepare for planning work.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a way she can act on.
S3.quote: I've seen the drawings say one thing and the hole say another, and the hole is always right.
S3.fieldNote: Five years makes her plan a step up rather than hold on. She sees her knowledge of what's really under the street as her edge. Asking her mum for money is a line she'd cross, but reluctantly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years means no one has an excuse. The company should be training people now and the government should be planning for what comes after. I'd say that in the union newsletter and I'd say it at the dinner table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be thirty-seven. That's enough time to get a diploma and maybe a few years in planning, and then see what's left. I think I'd be okay, honestly, if I start in the next year or two and don't just drift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still do the diploma, but slower, one evening a week so I'm not exhausted in the hole the next day. I'd stay a jointer for the first few years and save what I can. I'd want the union to set up a proper transition plan with the company, not just a leaflet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. There's a worry at the back, but it's background noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you'd drift, like you said?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big risk. I know myself. Ten years sounds like loads of time, and that's exactly how you end up at thirty-six with nothing done. I'd need a date on the calendar, like I start the course in September, no excuses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change anything else in your life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably where I live. If I go into planning, the jobs are at head office in the city, an hour away. I might move there eventually, but not until I had to.

S4.say: Ten years means nobody has an excuse: the company should train people now and the government should plan for afterwards. She'd say it in the union newsletter and at the dinner table.
S4.think: She'd be 37 at the end, with time for a diploma and some years in planning. She thinks she'd be fine if she starts soon and doesn't drift.
S4.do: Starts the diploma at one evening a week while staying a jointer for the first few years, saving what she can. Pushes the union for a real transition plan with the company.
S4.feel: Mostly uneasy, with a worry that stays in the background.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds like loads of time, and that's exactly how you end up at thirty-six with nothing done.
S4.fieldNote: Her biggest risk in the long timeline is herself: drifting because ten years feels endless. She'd set a hard start date. A later move to the city for planning work is possible but not something she'd rush.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. What would help is two things: a wage guarantee for people who get pushed out, paid for by the companies saving the money, and the company paying for proper training now, like it used to. And fix my pay grade while they're at it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about being a woman in this, and it matters. It took me years to be trusted in the hole. If the trade disappears just as women finally get in, that's a door slammed right after we got a foot through it.

headlineQuote: If the trade disappears just as women finally get in, that's a door slammed right after we got a foot through it.
portrait: Nora is a 27-year-old underground cable jointer on the old town network, proud of careful work she compares to surgery with a hacksaw. She shares a house, has about two weeks of savings, and is angry about a pay grade split that leaves her two hundred a month behind colleagues. She uses a chatbot now and then and will learn new kit once it has 'survived a winter in a hole'. She is calm about AI Plateau and uneasy about Steady Disruption, but AGI by 2028 has her doing rent sums at two in the morning. Given five or ten years, she'd study part-time for network planning, though she worries she might drift.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because with two weeks of savings and rent at forty percent of her pay she couldn't keep her room after the second month.
whatWouldHelp: A wage guarantee for people pushed out, paid for by the companies that save the money, plus company-paid training now and a fix to her pay grade.
